title: Wayne
name: Wayne
metaDescription: 1031 exchange coordination for Lancaster Avenue professional office and downtown retail in Wayne, Radnor Township, Pennsylvania.

sections.html: Wayne sits along the Lancaster Avenue corridor in Radnor Township, a Main Line submarket that has grown up around a small downtown retail strip and a run of standalone professional office buildings serving the surrounding household wealth and Villanova University's presence just to the west. Vacancy here runs lower than most of the surrounding suburbs, and that scarcity shows up directly in price, which changes how patient an investor can afford to be once a suitable property appears.

sections.heading: Lancaster Avenue Office Serves Professional Practices, Not Corporate Campuses
sections.html: Smaller standalone office buildings along the corridor lease to law firms, wealth management practices, and medical or dental offices rather than a single large corporate tenant, and lease terms tend to run shorter than a corporate headquarters deal. Tenant-improvement costs here are specific to professional-office buildout, exam rooms and reception layouts for a medical tenant rather than open-plan corporate space, and a buyer should confirm which specific improvements transfer with the building versus which belong to the departing tenant.

sections.heading: Downtown Retail Runs on a Tight, Walkable Footprint
sections.html: Wayne's small retail strip serves daytime office workers and nearby residents, storefront turnover is low, and available space rarely sits vacant long given how many buyers watch this corridor. Genuine competition among buyers for available inventory is a real factor an investor should expect rather than a market where patience alone wins a good deal, and a listing that lingers more than a few weeks is worth a closer look at why it has not already sold.

sections.heading: Villanova Proximity Shapes Some, Not All, of the Demand
sections.html: University-adjacent retail and service tenants cluster closer to the campus edge, while office and medical space deeper into Wayne's core draws more on the surrounding residential wealth than on the university's enrollment cycle. An investor should avoid overweighting university-driven demand for a property that sits well outside the immediate campus-adjacent blocks, since the two demand drivers do not extend equally across the whole submarket.

sections.heading: Diligence Given Thin Inventory and High Price Points
sections.html:
Because Wayne's inventory is scarce relative to buyer demand, a diligence file for replacement property here typically includes:

  • Rent roll and lease-term review for professional office tenants
  • Tenant-improvement allowance history for medical or dental space
  • Parking availability and easement review for downtown retail parcels
  • Zoning confirmation with Radnor Township for any proposed use change
  • Comparable sales pulled from similar Main Line professional-office submarkets

Given how quickly good listings move here, having this checklist ready before a property comes to market puts an investor in a stronger position than starting the review after an offer is already accepted.

sections.heading: What a Careful Wayne Exchange Looks Like
sections.html: Investors who succeed in this submarket separate university-driven demand from the broader residential-wealth demand that supports most of Wayne's office and retail, and they move decisively once suitable inventory appears rather than waiting for a second option that may not materialize given how thin this market runs. Preparation ahead of the identification window matters more here than in a market with a deeper pool of available comparables, and an investor who waits until day thirty to start reviewing available Wayne inventory is likely starting from a thinner list than one who began the search the day the relinquished property went under contract.

faqs.q: Does Villanova University drive most of the commercial demand in Wayne?
faqs.a: University-adjacent retail and service tenants benefit directly from campus proximity, but office and medical space further into Wayne's core draws more from the surrounding residential wealth, so demand should not be attributed to the university alone across the whole submarket.

faqs.q: Why does Wayne have lower vacancy than nearby suburbs?
faqs.a: Inventory here is genuinely limited relative to buyer and tenant demand, which keeps vacancy low and price per square foot high compared with many surrounding submarkets.

faqs.q: What tenant-improvement costs should I expect for medical office space in Wayne?
faqs.a: Medical and dental tenants typically require plumbing, exam-room layout, and specialized electrical work beyond a standard office buildout, and these costs are usually reflected in a larger allowance and longer lease term than a comparable office lease.

faqs.q: How should I handle identification given how few Wayne properties come to market?
faqs.a: Given thin annual transaction volume, the 200% rule can offer more flexibility than the three-property rule, allowing more candidates to be named as long as their combined value stays within the cap.

faqs.q: Should I be concerned if a Wayne listing has sat on the market for weeks?
faqs.a: Given how quickly desirable inventory typically moves in this submarket, a listing that lingers is worth a closer look at title, condition, or pricing issues that may not be obvious from the marketing materials alone.

faqs.q: Can this service confirm whether my Wayne property qualifies for 1031 treatment?
faqs.a: No. This service coordinates identification and communication among the investor's advisors. A qualifying determination is made by the investor's own CPA, tax attorney, and qualified intermediary.

faqs.q: Is Wayne a realistic submarket for an investor exchanging out of a much larger relinquished property?
faqs.a: It can be, but given the corridor's small building sizes, an investor moving substantial exchange value may need to identify several Wayne-area properties or pair a Wayne acquisition with a property elsewhere in the metro rather than relying on a single small building alone.

faqs.q: Does Wayne's proximity to other Main Line towns change how I should compare listings?
faqs.a: Comparables should still be pulled from towns with a similar mix of professional office and walkable retail rather than assuming every Main Line submarket prices the same way, since scarcity and tenant demand vary meaningfully from one station stop to the next.
